ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Some of the small squares on each of the square transparencies have been coloured black. If you slide the three transparencies on top of each other, without lifting them from the table, a new pattern can be seen. What is the maximum number of black squares which could be seen in the new pattern?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure has three side-by-side transparent 3×3 grid sheets. Number by rows from top to bottom and by columns from left to right. The black squares on the left transparent sheet are at (1,1), (1,2), (3,2), (3,3). The black squares on the middle transparent sheet are at (1,2), (1,3), (3,1). The black squares on the right transparent sheet are at (2,2), (2,3), (3,1), (3,2). Reasoning: The problem says to slide the three transparent sheets together without lifting them from the table, so the orientation does not change, and the corresponding 3×3 squares can be compared. After they are stacked together, as long as any one transparent sheet is black at a position, that square will ultimately appear black. Take the union of the three sets: {(1,1),(1,2),(3,2),(3,3)} ∪ {(1,2),(1,3),(3,1)} ∪ {(2,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2)} = {(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2),(3,3)}. This includes 8 different squares, and only (2,1) does not appear. Therefore at most 8 black small squares can be seen.

From the text, use that the transparencies are slid on top of one another without being lifted, so their orientation is unchanged and corresponding grid cells can be compared directly. A cell in the final pattern is black if at least one of the three transparencies has black in that cell. Take the union of the listed black-cell positions: all cells except (2,1) occur, giving 8 black squares.

method.method_draft: Instead of counting black cells directly, inspect which final cells could remain white. From the image, compare the three 3 by 3 transparencies cell by cell. A final square stays white only if that same cell is white on all three transparencies. Reading the diagrams, the middle-left cell, row 2 column 1, is white on all three. Every other one of the 9 positions is black on at least one transparency. Therefore the overlaid pattern can have at most 9 - 1 = 8 black squares, and this bound is achieved by stacking them in the shown orientation.
